result.markdown: --- gd-head-tags: - >- ``{=html} open-graph: title: >- [Graph.antichains()]{.doc-object-name .doc-function .doc-label .doc-label-method} | Edgecase description: List every antichain of a directed acyclic graph. twitter-card: title: >- [Graph.antichains()]{.doc-object-name .doc-function .doc-label .doc-label-method} | Edgecase description: List every antichain of a directed acyclic graph. title: >- [Graph.antichains()]{.doc-object-name .doc-function .doc-label .doc-label-method} body-classes: doc-api-page doc-py-api-page shift-heading-level-by: 0 bread-crumbs: false toc-depth: 3 description-meta: List every antichain of a directed acyclic graph. page-navigation: false html-table-processing: none --- ::: {.doc-subject} List every antichain of a directed acyclic graph. ::: ::: {.doc-usage-source} Usage [Source](https://github.com/rich-iannone/edgecase/blob/main/python/edgecase/graph.py#L58217-L58301){target="_blank" rel="noopener"} ::: ::: {.doc-signature .doc-function} ```pythonsignature Graph.antichains(topo_order=None) ``` ::: ::: {.doc-text} ![Antichains](../assets/graphs/antichains.light.svg){.lightbox fig-alt="A diamond DAG: A points to B and C, which both point to D. B and C, in the accent color, cannot reach each other, so together they form the largest antichain; every other pair lies on a common path. The card lists all six antichains in the order returned: the empty set, D, C, B, then B and C (accent), then A." width="100%"} An antichain is a set of nodes no two of which are comparable: neither can reach the other along directed paths. In a task dependency graph, an antichain is a set of tasks that can run in parallel; in a partial order (a version history, a taxonomy), it is a set of mutually unrelated elements. The empty set is an antichain too. By Dilworth's theorem, the size of the largest antichain equals the fewest chains needed to cover the order. The number of antichains can be exponential, so use it on small DAGs. ::: ## Parameters {.doc-parameters} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [topo_order]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [list[Union[int, str]] | None]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [None]{.doc-parameter-default} : Optional topological order (IDs or labels) to drive the enumeration. If `None` (default), `topological_sort()` is used. ::: ## Returns {.doc-returns} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [list[list[int]]]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : Every antichain as a list of node IDs, starting with the empty one. ::: ## Raises {.doc-raises} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [ValueError]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : If the graph is not a directed acyclic graph. ::: ## Technical Notes {.doc-technical-notes} Depth-first extension along the topological order: an antichain is extended by any later node that is incomparable with all of its members, using the transitive closure for the comparability test (Freese, 2004). Matches NetworkX's `antichains` for the same order. ## Examples {.doc-examples} In a diamond A -> B, A -> C, B -> D, C -> D, only B and C are incomparable, so the antichains are the empty set, the four single nodes, and {B, C}: ::: {#f6b1aba0 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.python .cell-code} import edgecase as ec g = ec.Graph(directed=True).add_nodes(["A", "B", "C", "D"]) g.add_edges([("A", "B"), ("A", "C"), ("B", "D"), ("C", "D")]) [[g.get_label_from_id(n) for n in a] for a in g.antichains()] ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` [[], ['D'], ['C'], ['B'], ['B', 'C'], ['A']] ``` ::: :::
